subtopic: THIRD AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE APPOINTED TO INQUIRE INTO THE OPERATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT

speechtext:
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS FOULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, the special committee appointed to inquire into the operation of the

Civil Service Committee Report
Civil Service Act begs to present the following as its third and final report.
Pursuant to order of reference dated February 22, your committee has held forty-eight sittings, has examined the three civil service commissioners, the secretary of the civil service commission, the chief, the acting chief and investigators Boutin and Jackson of the organization branch, and the chief examiner of the civil service commission; heard representations from Sir Francis Floud, K.C.B., K.C.M.G., United Kingdom high commissioner in Canada, the professional institute of the civil service, the civil service federation of Canada, the amalgamated civil servants of Canada, the dominion railway mail clerks federation, the amputations association of the great war and the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. Briefs were received from army and navy veterans in Canada, officers, mates and petty officers of government ships, the Canadian postmasters' association, the customs and excise officers' association, and the New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island nautical association.
Your committee had charts prepared showing the organization of the staffs of the civil service commission and all departments of the government whose staff are under the civil service commission, hut was unable, in the time at its disposal, to make an extensive inquiry into the various departments.
Having carefully considered the evidence adduced, your committee recommends:
1.	Your committee deems it expedient and in the interest of the public, the civil service and the civil service commission that a standing committee on civil service matters be appointed at the commencement of each session of parliament, and therefore recommends to parliament that standing order 63 be amended by adding after clause (k) of said order, the following clause (1): "on civil service matters to consist of fifteen members, nine of whom shall constitute a quorum."
2.	The committee further recommends that no official or employee in the civil service shall make any direct or indirect recommendation or reference by letter or otherwise on behalf of any relative by blood or marriage, or take any part whether directly or indirectly in any competition, temporary or permanent assignment, promotion, classification or reclassification in which any such relative is an applicant.
3.	Your committee recommends that it shall he the duty of the civil service commission to make their own rulings on the operation of the act and apply the same uniformly, provided, however, that any department affected by such ruling may join the civil service commission in any submission to the Department of Justice for an opinion.
4.	Your committee reaffirms the eighteenth recommendation of the civil service committee of 1932, which is as follows:
"18. Your committee is of opinion that there is a great deal of overlapping in the performance of duties by the heads of different branches of the civil service commission, owing to matters receiving the attention of the secretary of the commission which are in no way related to secretarial duties."
"Your committee, therefore, recommends that the secretary of the civil service commission be
called upon to perform only those duties which are peculiarly those of a secretary and that the civil service commission consider ways and means of eliminating duplication of correspondence and departmental memoranda which now pass through the secretary to the commissioners."
And your committee recommends that all forms presently in use for such purposes shall be altered accordingly.
5.	As the multiplicity of classifications and the discrepancy in salary ranges tend to create jealousy in the service and have resulted ir injustices and dissatisfaction, your committee suggests that the service should be divided intc five or six broad classes, with a maximum ol not more than nine grades in one class, anc such division to be set up as soon as possible.
6.	From the evidence it appears there is at present a considerable discrepancy in salary ranges as between departments and as between the various branches of the same department and as between the Senate and House of Commons, which militates against efficiency and cooperation, your committee recommends that the organization branch be charged with special responsibility with regard to salary levels in order to simplify ranges and also to thoroughly investigate salaries paid in comparable classes within and without the service.
7.	Your committee recommends that
(1)	Annual surveys of departments, units or branches shall be made in rotation by the various investigators, whether requested by the department or not, and such reviews shall be made so as to remedy overlapping, overstaffing or understaffing and any unfair discrepancies which may exist.
(2)	If there is to be specialization, it shall be within classes rather than by attempting to cover a whole department from top to bottom, as at present.
(3)	Investigators shall mention in each report the time spent with each employee and the date and circumstances of the interviews.
(4)	Investigators shall not sit on examining boards as members thereof.
8.	In order to give the civil service commissioners a complete picture which will ensure fairness and department responsibility, and which will standardize the service and speed up the handling of cases, your committee recommends that the investigator's report and organization branch chief's comments be forwarded to department concerned and returned to the civil service commission with any comments such department wishes to make.
9.	Your committee recommends that no married women shall be employed even temporarily under her maiden name and regulation No. 36 of the civil service commission shall be strictly applied.
10.	Your committee recommends that subsection one of section 38 of the Civil Service Act be amended by adding at the end thereof the following proviso:
"Provided that,_ except on approval by the governor general in council, such authorization shall not extend to the employment of a person who is not a natural born or naturalized British subject and also has been a resident of Canada for at least five years."
11.	Your committee recommends the commission may, at the request of the department con-

Civil Service Committee Report
cerned, but subject to the approval of the treasury board, appoint without competition any person who has already held a permanent position in the civil service and who has resigned, to the same or a similar position within the department if the department and the commission are satisfied that such person is deserving of such appointment, is not over fifty-five years of age, is of good character and in good physical condition.
12.	Your committee recommends that standard advertisements to cover the classes and grades suggested in its fifth recommendation should be prepared and adhered to and that the practice which has often been followed in the past of writing advertisements to fit the qualifications of a single individual should be discontinued. Your committee recommends further that any reason for varying such standard advertisements should be submited in writing by the deputy-head suggesting such variation and be reported thereon by the organization branch and that no such varied advertisement shall be issued or published unless previously approved by the civil service commission.
13.	Your committee recommends that examination papers should not be translated for examination purposes but should be read by the examiners in the language in which they have been written, whether English or French.
14.	Your committee is of the opinion that
whenever advisable transfers to other branches of departments, as well as from one department to another, should be encouraged so as to prevent favoritism and for the purpose of helping employees to acquire a general knowledge of the work of the department or departments of the government. Your committee considers that the effect of this recommendation will be to open new horizons to the younger employees by offering opportunities for advancement and promotion at the same time preventing the static condition of the service and remedying certain injustices.	_
15.	To facilitate the adjustments of complaints of a civil servant, where such complaints cannot otherwise be adjusted, your committee recommends that such complaints be adjudicated by a board of appeal consisting of a nominee of a civil service organization named by the appellant, a nominee of the deputy head of the department affected, and a nominee _ of the chairman of the civil service commission, the latter of whom shall be chairman of the board.
16.	Your committee recommends that ratings on efficiency and fitness, on which selections for promotion are largely based, be made by a board of three departmental officers instead of by individual departmental officers, as at present, and that a system of periodical ratings recording the efficiency of employees be established, for use in connection with promotions, salary increases and retirements. That the employee shall be advised of the result of all his ratings and shall have right to appeal such rating to the board mentioned in the preceding recommendation.
17.	Your committee recommends that promotions shall not be confirmed until after the expiration of fourteen days so as to permit the making of an appeal to the board mentioned in your committee's fifteenth recommendation, and in the event of such appeal being made that such promotion shall not be confirmed until the appeal has been disposed of.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
18.	Your committee recommends that the practice of placing employees in vacant positions in an acting capacity instead of holding promotion competitions for them be discouraged.
19.	Your committee recommends that the commission investigate the feasibility of more extensive and adequate advertising of competitions by press and radio.
20.	Your committee regrets that the recommendation of the civil service committee of 1932 "that all papers, documents, et cetera, placed on the files of the commission, be consecutively numbered in each file, so that removals or deletions therefrom will be apparent" has been ignored, and recommends that it shall be strictly observed and that also each document on file shall be duly initialed and dated.
21.	Your committee recommends that section twenty-one of the Civil Service Act, dealing with vacancies in the departments, be amended by providing (in subsection two thereof) for the case of temporary appointments when there is no eligible list that: "the commission shall forthwith hold an examination and, if necessary, to prevent any serious interference with the public business, but not_ otherwise, may fill the position at once, subject to the approval of the head of the department, by making a temporary appointment as prescribed herein," the only change in the subsection being the insertion therein of the words italicized above.
22.	Your committee is of the opinion that the preference granted by section twenty-eight and twenty-nine of the act to persons who have served overseas in the military or naval forces of His Majesty's allies shall apply only when such persons are natural born or naturalized British subjects, and also had been resident in Canada before the great war.
23.	Your committee recommends that no male employee shall be retained in the civil service beyond the age of sixty-five years and no female employee beyond the age of sixty years, and that such retirement be made compulsory without any extension.
Your committee is of the opinion that this would materially increase the efficiency of the civil service, would facilitate promotion and create a brighter outlook for the future of the younger people in the service or desirous of entering therein.	.
24.	Your committee is of the opinion that a departmental division of eighty per cent permanent and twenty per cent temporary results in discrimination in certain branches where the work is entirely permanent and where twenty per cent have to wait years for any hope of permanency, and also that further evil of this system is that a branch may pad up work to bring in extra temporaries, so as to absorb into the permanent quota those who otherwise would not be permanent.
25.	Your committee recommends that long term temporaries on the staff of the House of Commons who have been giving satisfactory service for a number of years should be made permanent employees under the civil service commission.
And that the evidence taken by the committee be indexed and one thousand copies in English and five hundred copies in French be printed in bluebook form.

A copy of the minutes of proceedings and evidence taken is tabled herewith; also three exhibits filed on May 25.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Jean-Frangois Pouliot,
Chairman.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO TERMS AND OPERATION OF SUPERANNUATION ACT- THIRD REPORT CONCURRED IN

speechtext: Mr. MALCOLM McLEAN (Melfort) moved that the third and final report of the special committee appointed to inquire into terms and operations of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, presented to the house on June 28, be concurred in.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO TERMS AND OPERATION OF SUPERANNUATION ACT- THIRD REPORT CONCURRED IN
speechtext:
I
want to say only a few words on this report. I know how invidious it is for a member who has taken no part in the work of a committee to criticize the results of their faithful labour, and I do not want to put myself in that false position. But I must express, on behalf of those whom I more immediately represent in connection with the matter, my disappointment that the report is not more definite than it is. If I remember rightly, this is the third committee on this subject in the last five or six years. They have all made the same indefinite kind of report, and each of them has ended in just nothing being done. I believe one committee recommended that the departmental officials should look into it. Time is going on; most of these people are getting old, and they are looking forward hopefully, or almost hopelessly now, to some arrangement being made so that they can come under the superannuation act. The people I more immediately refer to are the masters and mates and petty officers of the government boats. There is no reason in the world why they should not, and many reasons why they should, be allowed to come under superannuation. They put in petitions year after year. I myself have been privy to at least three of them. Now the best we get is to have the committee recommend that a similar committee be set up to continue the inquiry next session. I make no reflection on the work of the committee. They seem to have carried on an extraordinary number of interviews, they have examined a large number of witnesses, and so on; but it is unfortunate that perhaps they were rather late in getting organized. I quite admit that it is now too late for the government to do anything this session, but I would suggest that either the chairman of the committee or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) might hold out some hope of the committee being set up early next session in order to present in ample
Questions
time a concrete recommendation which the government could put into effect. If the months are allowed to pass and another committee is appointed it will have to begin de novo and go over the same evidence again, and a year from now we shall be in the same position. We shall again find that the report of the committee will come down too late for the government to take action. I earnestly urge upon the government that they make a note of this so as to have the committee set up early next session in order that we may have some definite recommendation which might be acted upon.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REDUCTION OP RATES FROM MILLING POINTS TO PACIFIC COAST

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REDUCTION OP RATES FROM MILLING POINTS TO PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Concerning the agreement between the railway companies and the government for reduced rates on mill feed from milling points to coast points may I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) whether such reduced rates apply to carload lots for the benefit of farmers and poultryimen along the Columbia river in West Kootenay district? Further, does the government accept the declaration of the railways that if intermediate points insist upon reduced rates the railways will cancel the rates to the coast?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REDUCTION OP RATES FROM MILLING POINTS TO PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The only part taken by the government in the matter referred to by my hon. friend was to pass on to parliament an offer from the railways to meet the wishes of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), who brought the situation before the house. The railways offered to include mill feeds in the feed grain rates covered by the agreement of 1933, and I passed that offer on to parliament. The railway offer provided that the same rates that apply in the movement of mill feeds under an arrangement made in 1933 will apply as the maximum rate on mill feeds moving from points outside British Columbia into British Columbia.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue-for the Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 174, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain expenditures made and indebtedness incurred by the Canadian National Railways system during the calendar year 1938, and to authorize the guarantee by his majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Section one agreed to.
On section 2-Power to issue securities for refunding and capital expenditures.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
There is nothing here to indicate that it is capital expenditures. The minister yesterday made it clear that we were coming within that provision of our general rule by providing capital for the road. This is not providing for deficits or for deficiency of revenues to meet ordinary, everyday maintenance charges, but for capital charges. Should that not appear in section 2, so as to have it read:
. . . approved to provide the amounts necessary to meet in whole or in part capital expenditures made or indebtedness incurred on capital account during the calendar year 1938
That would be in accordance with the principles that govern Canadian National financing.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES
speechtext: Paragraphs (a) and (b) make it clear that those are capital expenditures.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES
speechtext: Subparagraph (a) does, but (b) does not. In the details as given yesterday the word " capital " was used in one case, and inferred in another. The down payment on certain equipment might be regarded as a capital expenditure. It has been the custom-I cannot say whether it has continued-to charge the instalments due each year on purchase price to operating revenues. They may buy a locomotive for $100,000, pay $25,000 cash, and the other $75,000 is represented by securities which mature over a period of years. The general rule has been- it may be changed now-to retire them out of earnings. I think that is what the interstate commerce commission approved and what we adopted. It would appear reasonable that the expenditures involved in the use of the locomotive for the business should be charged against operating revenues.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES
speechtext: While that is the principle of amortization behind the Philadelphia plan, nevertheless the twenty-five per cent payment is a capital expenditure. It seems to me unnecessary to put in the word " capital "; the fact is it is capital. But there can be no objection to doing so.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES
speechtext: We laid down this rule with respect to capital and other expenditures on the road, that the country assumes responsibility for the capital expenditures. It is well to keep that line of demarcation clearly before us. If we provide $50,000,000 for deficits, that is one thing; if we provide $15,000,000 for capital, that is another, and we should make that clear in the statutes so that those who desire to study the general situation may have no difficulty in ascertaining what is capital and what is not. I am not concerned about it other than for that reason.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND INDEBTEDNESS, AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES
speechtext: I hardly think it necessary, because the section refers to the "following accounts," and the accounts are set out in considerable detail. There can be no question about the purpose to which the money is to be applied.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, June 28, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Lapointe-Mr. Sanderson in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to incorporate a commission with power under the Minister of Justice to administer, control and manage the penitentiaries; to provide for salaries of the commissioners and assistant com-

missioners and to amend and consolidate the Penitentiaries Act and amending acts and repeal the same.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
Last evening I was dealing with the report of this commission on the Buck case. Before I conclude what I have to say in that regard I think I should refer to the judgment of the Supreme Court of Ontario, reported in volume 3, Dominion Law Reports, page 98. I do that for one purpose only, namely to point out how serious this matter was in the judgment of Chief Justice Mulock. He points out with very great care that this man had openly advocated the very thing which he was charged with doing in that penitentiary. And now to re-try this case in the sense that it has been re-tried in this report does violence to one's understanding and appreciation, I think, of the whole theory under which commissions operate and act. For instance, Chief Justice Mulock refers to the evidence given by Buck himself, and at page 102 he says:
According to the evidence of the accused Timothy Buck, large numbers of communists in Canada, in the fall of 1920, secured copies of those theses and statutes and in 1921 several groups of communists held a conference in Canada and formed an association called the communist party of Canada. Buck testified that the communist party of Canada was a section of the communist international, and that from the year 1924 onward the above named theses and statutes became binding upon the communist party of Canada.
Those words in themselves were very serious, and they were the considered words of the chief justice of Ontario, Sir William Mulock.

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext: May I ask the date of that?

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext: This was in 1932, just before Buck was actually sent to prison, on the case that was presented to the court of appeal in the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext: What has that to do with the report of the commission?

subtopic: INCORPORATION OF COMMISSION FOR ADMINISTRATION, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT-AMENDMENT OF EXISTING ACTS
speechtext:
I am now dealing with the penitentiaries report and the Buck case. The language used at page 103 is this:
-the communist party to join systematically, lawful and unlawful work, lawful and unlawful organizations ... It is especially necessary to carry on unlawful work in the army and navy, police . . . and persistent and systematic propaganda and agitation if necessary in the army where communist groups should be formed in every military organization.
That was part of it. Then he proceeds:
Such mass demonstrations are prepared and carried out by the organized masses of the proletariat under the direction of the united, disciplined, centralized communist party. Civil war is war. In this war the proletariat must

Penitentiaries Commission Act
have its efficient political officers, its good political general staff to conduct operations during all the stages of that fight.
Then, follow references to other points of the same character, and I-direct attention to this matter particularly:
In every country where, in consequence of martial law or of other exceptional laws the communists are unable to carry on their work legally, a combination of legal and illegal work is absolutely necessary . . . But refusal to carry on or to participate in such work should be considered equal to treason to the revolutionary cause and incompatible with affiliation to the Third International.
I need not trouble to read further references, but the decision of that court resulted in this man being sent to Kingston penitentiary. Then riots occurred on two occasions, to which reference is made in this report; and during the quelling of one of those riots, with the aid of the militia, the shots to which I referred last night were fired. A report was made by two inspectors and by the superintendent, and six years later this commission makes a report which did not involve the calling of eye witnesses, as did the other case, but which enabled those who were the proponents of the faith of Buck to make the allegations that have been made from time to time in recent months.
I now proceed to what I regard as the most important point in connection with the report of this commission. I should like to ask the minister just where the authority was given to this commission to investigate the day to day operations of these penitentiaries. That is a matter for the minister, through his superintendent. I look at the order in council, for which the minister made the recommendation, and that order in council says that the commission is to inquire into and report upon-
-the penal system of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing, the following matters:
1. The treatment of convicted persons in the penitentiaries, covering the investigation and examination of the classification of the institutions;
As to that we have some evidence and something in the report, but that does not involve the question of the trial of the officials who, under the Civil Sendee Act, are responsible to their chief and to the department over which the right hon. gentleman presides.
The classification of offenders;
The construction of penal institutions;
The organization of penal departments;
The appointment of staffs;
The treatment to be accorded to the different classes of offenders, including corporal and other punishment;
The protection of society;
Reformative and rehabilitative treatment;
Employment of prisoners;
Prison labour;
Remuneration;
The study of international standard minimum rules, and other subjects cognate to the above.
2.	The administration, management, discipline and police of penitentiaries.
Surely that does not cover dealing with the individual men in the penitentiaries. That is a matter for the minister, and, as I said yesterday, we have substituted for the minister and his control the work of this commission.
3.	Cooperation between governmental and social agencies in the prevention of crime, including juvenile delinquency, and the furnishing of aid to prisoners upon release from imprisonment.
4.	The conditional release of prisoners, including parole or release on probation, conditional release under the Ticket of Leave Act, and remission generally.
Then the order in council was amended for the purpose of appointing Mr. McRuer in place of Mr. Anderson. I want to point out just one more fact in that connection. Under these provisions you have the public destruction of the value of many tried and experienced officials. I am sure the minister never intended that this should be done. The minister never intended that these men should go into these institutions and pick out John Smith, Peter Jones and so on, and say, "We do not like the way these people do their work," because the doing of that by this public commission has destroyed the usefulness of these men, who are public servants, responsible to the minister and to the government of the day. This commission having made this report has made it extremely difficult for these men to continue to function.
I will give another case; I gave some last evening and if I so desired I could go through this report and take them one after the other, to show that there was no power contemplated on the part of this commission to deal with these matters in this way. Least of all I think did the minister expect it to be done. No one who participated in the discussion that occurred in this house ever thought we were to do that.
Now I take another case, at page 296, in connection with the chaplain and religious services at Kingston. The chaplain there was Reverend Mr. Kidd, who, unfortunately, happened to be -the brother of the local member for that constituency. Why should he be brought into this and singled out to be treated in this way? Why should any of the chaplains be treated in this way? But the commission say:
Several complaints were made that the Protestant chaplain lacked the proper personality and approach to the men and that he was unable to gain their confidence. While
Penitentiaries Commission Act

your commissioners believe that he is earnest in his work, we do not find the same evidence of results as we found in some other penitentiaries. It is very important that chaplains should possess the ability to secure the confidence of the inmates if they are to be able to influence them.
The reports of the people who know Mr. Kidd, who was a padre overseas, are absolutely at variance with that statement. What is the position of the Minister of Justice in this matter? Here he has in front of him individuals dealt with by name. He himself has these recommendations or statements made about them, and yet he cannot remove them from office, unless it be under the section which says that it is in the interests of efficiency of the institution that they should be removed. And the commission go all through these penitentiaries, one after the other, and take the wardens, the deputy wardens, the guards, the inspectors and the chaplains, and deal with them one after the other. I ask the minister if that was the purpose of this investigation. That was not my understanding of it, or of any application that was made. It was to deal with the large and broad problem of prison administration-in detail, as the minister has pointed out-the question whether or not the proper form of administration prevailed and whether or not the chaplain's services are desirable. In the Saskatchewan penitentiary, where there is a full time Protestant chaplain, they say he does not visit the cells. Not visiting the cells, he has the prisoners paraded before him. They may have questions to ask and complaints to make. That was a recent appointment of a full time official. The same is said with respect to the Roman Catholic chaplain, namely that he does not go to the cells to see them.
I must ask the Minister of Justice if that is the sort of thing he thought this commission was going to deal with. That is a matter of internal administration, a matter for the minister's own guidance, not something which should be made public in this sense, thus destroying the entire usefulness of it. Man after man is picked out and dealt with in this report, one after the other. We may take the case of Dawson, to whom I referred last night. He is a returned man, who served with the Canadian expeditionary force. He was an accountant, and they say they do not think he is a particularly good man to be an inspector. That is the sort of thing that goes on through this whole document.
I ask again, can we adequately deal with this matter without having the opportunity to study the evidence? And listen to the kind of evidence that was taken, according to the report itself, not what I say about it.

I quote:
At the outset, your commissioners decided to give all the inmates and officers of the various penitentiaries the fullest opportunity to make any representations they wished, pertaining either to their own welfare or to conditions existing in the different institutions, and, in order to ensure this by removing any fear as to the consequences which might result from freedom in expressing their views, the commission decided not to engage outside counsel, that the sittings should be held in camera, and that, while inmates were giving evidence, no penitentiary officer would be permitted to attend.
That is the sort of thing that we find. I visited the penitentiary at Kingston with the then Minister of Justice, without notice, and I asked various prisoners why they were there, what their previous condition had been, where they had come from. I can remember only one who said to me, "I am here because I ought to be here." Most of them said it was a frame-up or that someone had done something to get them there. I must say to the Minister of Justice that in ninety cases out of a hundred-well, perhaps not ninety, but at least eighty

the accused give evidence. If they are convicted, in addition to the other offences with which they are charged, they are perjurers, because a judge or a jury has not believed their statements made under oath; and they are now brought in here, free from any surroundings which may control or limit their activities, and permitted to tell their tale. And on that we have these men-these hard working men-treated in this way. Is it fair? Is it right or just?
Surely it was not intended that that ever should be the duty of this commission. Obviously the commission has entirely gone outside of its order of reference. What is more, and one of the regrettable things, long before this report came in it was known that they were going to get Ormond, that they were going to get Dawson, and others named in the report-an absolute negation of the purpose for which the commission was constituted. It was to report upon the penal system, and to deal with matters the minister now deals with. Think how much more difficult it has been made for the minister. Charged as he is with an enormous responsibility in connection with the penal institutions of this country, he is now handicapped by reports made public with respect to men on the evidence of inmates given in the manner indicated, all of whom have been convicted by the courts of the country, and the majority of whom are also perjurers-found as such either by the juries or by the courts. Is that right, or just, or fair?

Penitentiaries Commission Act
Who were these men? Some of the men I saw had been convicted of murder, and their sentences had been commuted to life imprisonment. Others had committed offences against the person, such as assault and attempted murder and rape. In this list you have forgers, men who violated the criminal law with respect to embezzlement, theft, and matters of the kind. And these men come in here by invitation and make their statements in camera, without the presence of anyone connected with the administration. You take the names of the officials mentioned in the report and you say, "We do not think so and so is doing his job as fully as he might." That is a matter for the minister and the superintendent to decide. That is a matter of discipline. See what we have done: we have made it that much more difficult for the Minister of Justice to discharge his heavy duties and obligations.
I pointed out the other day that the first time I remembered Kingston being mentioned in the house was in connection with the penitentiary. At that time they were dealing with problems, and demanded a commission. They got the commission, to which reference is made in the report. That commission made its report with respect to certain matters. Then there was another commission on which Mr. Biggar, K.C., sat, and that commission made its report. Mr. Biggar was one of the committee who recommended . that General Ormond should be appointed. Now we have the present report. Kingston has always been looming large with respect to discussions of penitentiary conditions. I ask the minister this:	Were these men experts on the kind
of buildings that should be built? And yet I find the commission complaining bitterly about the change of construction in the women's building at Kingston. They say the architectural plans have been changed. They say further that Collin's Bay cost too much money and is too elaborately got up. Now, the Minister of Justice was the gentleman who was responsible for the setting up of Collin's Bay. They make this reflection upon that work. It was carried on by the next government, and is being completed by the present government. The women's building was designed by the best men available, and then alterations were made in it. I refer to the building at Kingston. That is set out at length.
That building, too, was commenced not by the late government or the present government. And there you have running through it this web of interference with respect to all these matters, setting up the judgment of 51952-277
three men, without any evidence as to their knowledge or ability to deal with it, as to the construction of a building and matters of that kind. Is it fair or just that we should hand over this whole penal system to a commission, without having had at least some opportunity, not upon this evidence thus secured but upon what the minister and others know to be the facts, to consider the matter?
As to the complaint against men who have had military training, the minister is not to blame for that. The civil service commission appointed them, not the minister, and preference was given to returned men under the statute. The minister did not do that. Now they are complaining that the statutes of Canada are improperly enacted. This commission has said that these military men should not be there, that they are arrogant and that they bring militarism into the conduct of the penitentiaries. In the report that was read this morning with reference to the civil service, the only limitation placed upon appointments was that they should not be of people who were bora outside of Canada. But so far as I know both these men against whom complaints are being made were born in Canada, and they gave service,
I do submit to the minister that we should not be asked to change the whole penal system of this country without any evidence that warrants it. In England, at Dartmoor and elsewhere, my observation is that the governors in most of these institutions are military men, and have been for years. In our country, until the great war came, there was, generally speaking, no military class from whom these men could be selected. The civil service commission has made all the appointments to the penitentiaries-I do not mean temporary clerks but appointments of importance-therefore the minister is not responsible.

I do not wish to do more than present what in my judgment as a member of this house I conceive to be one of the greatest difficulties we have had to meet in this regard, namely, the lack of opportunity to determine whether or not there is any evidence upon which action might be taken. Before the report came down the government had apparently made up its mind to take action. The government probably knew what the commission was doing, because the report was dated in April, but I had no knowledge until the report came down. I have looked at the recommendations, but I have had no time to read the report except casually, as I pointed out yesterday, and members of the

Penitentiaries Commission Act
house tell me that they have had no time to do more than read the introduction. None of us have seen the evidence, which we thought would be laid on the table of this house that we might consult it. No one suggests, least of all I, that we should go to the expense of printing it, but in the case of the commission dealing with the railways, the report was placed in the library and the appropriate place for this report would be to lay it on the table of the house that we might study it. The report of this commission, dealing with matters of great national concern, is apparently to result in an entire change in the penal system of this country. The minister says that the appointment of the three commissioners will not be partisan, that he will do his best to prevent that, but they must necessarily be political appointments, and that commission is to be the governing body of the penitentiaries of this country.
I say further that the minister has sustained my position; the act is to be brought into force by proclamation, thereby indicating that there is much to be done before these recommendations can be made effective. I suggest again, without of course any likelihood of its even being considered, in view of the position taken by the minister, that the interests of this nation would be best served by giving an opportunity for the people also to think about the recommendations made by that commission. It is usual to afford an opportunity for consideration of a report of this kind, and certainly there has been no opportunity for the public generally to investigate and consider the recommendations and to arrive at conclusions. I am not going to do more than make that statement again to the minister, knowing that, having taken the position he has, he cannot vary his view. But rarely have I known of any attempt being made to deal in this way with a matter of such great public importance-within fourteen days of the bringing down of the recommendation, to change a whole system which has been in existence since pre-confederation days, and then support this attitude, when we ask for further time, by saying that it will not go into force except by proclamation. No opportunity will be afforded between now and then for any changes to be made, because the statute itself will be conclusive upon every phase of penitentiary administration. I would think that many changes would have to be made in the Penitentiaries Act, that many changes would also have to be made in the whole setup of our penal system, and that these operations would take considerable time.

speechtext:
We have listened to a very long discussion of some phases of this report. As I listened last evening to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) dealing with the Kingston riots, it did not strike me that he was painting an accurate picture, as I understood that picture from the report, and therefore, at the risk of taking a little time when the committee does not wish time to be taken, I desire to deal particularly with that phase of it. Since last evening I have made a very careful study of the relevant pages in the report. I think this, that in the recommendation regarding the superintendent the commission was justified upon the evidence relating to the Price incident alone.
You will recollect from the report that during the penitentiary riot Price was shot in the right shoulder. The guards were called and told that a prisoner had been seriously wounded, indeed that he was dying. This, of course, proved to be exaggerated. The wounded man remained unattended in his cell for twenty-two hours, from October 20 to October 21, the bullet not being removed until October 23. Subsequently the wounded man was in hospital until December 1. There is no evidence given anywhere, either by the superintendent or by anyone else, to show that he endeavoured to place the responsibility for the firing of this shot or for the neglect to which this particular man was subjected, nor is there any reason given for the delay in giving Price medical treatment, in securing an X-ray photograph, or in the removal of the bullet until some days later. In his report to the Minister of Justice, on the contrary, the superintendent treated the incident as one of little account. I find on page 80 this report to the Minister of Justice:
One convict in the prison of isolation was struck in the shoulder by a bullet which ricochetted from the barrier. It was ascertained that he was not seriously injured.
That was the report made to the Minister of Justice by the superintendent. As I said a few moments ago, I believe it shows that he treated the incident lightly.
We have the commission's finding on the following page. After reviewing the evidence, this is what the commission said:
The commission find that the treatment accorded to this prisoner (Price) after he was wounded was brutal and inhuman. In addition to being allowed to remain in his cell for twenty-two hours without medical attention, he was given no surgical treatment until the third day after the shooting. In our opinion, the circumstances called for the most searching and careful investigation in order to fix responsibility both for the shooting and the subsequent neglect, as well as for strict disciplinary action when the responsibility

Penitentiaries Commission Act
had been fixed. The superintendent failed to do this, and, instead, issued a report to the minister, which eventually was made public, indicating that the wounding was of a trifling and accidental nature.
The leader of the opposition dealt at considerable length with the Buck case. I have looked into the evidence which was submitted to the commission, and find that the picture presented to us last evening was not an accurate representation of what occurred. Let us remember that the Buck case has not only been investigated by the commission; it was the subject of a trial before Judge Deroche, who delivered judgment on July 6, 1933. Last night the leader of the opposition quoted from the report which was made, almost a year after the riot, by inspectors Craig and Dawson, who were parties interested in more or less shielding themselves in connection with what occurred on -that particular occasion. In that report, the leader of the opposition contended, inspectors Dawson and Craig had stated that Buck admitted incitement to riot. Now, -that can not only be disputed, but it is not a statement of fact, as was found by a duly constituted court and by Judge Deroche.

And the questions and answers. I propose to read the judgment of Judge Deroche, before whom Buck came to trial for his participation in the Kingston riot. I take it that the leader of the opposition will agree with me that when a judge in a court tries a man and delivers judgment, that judgment, except upon appeal to a superior court, is unassailable, and at least is much better evidence than the kind of evidence which would be given by two inspectors who were interested in whitewashing themselves and the institution in connection with the incidents that occurred. I turn to page 81 of the report and. I read:
Buck was tried for his participation in the disturbance of October 17 before His Honour Judge Deroche, who delivered judgment on the 6th of July, 1933, in part as follows:
"Then I think I had better say this before I start my judgment proper. You presented to me-
He is addressing Buck.

a most unusual request in your argument this morning. Your request in so many words said 'I hope your honour can find me not guilty,
[Mr. ColdwellJ
but if you feel you must find me guilty, then there is something I prize even more than the question of guilt, and that is that my name may be cleared of having done or said some things which I deny, and which would stamp me in my own opinion as a blackguard.' I am very glad to say to you that I can clear you of these things. I do not believe you shut off the motor in your shop; I do not believe you spoke in the mail bag department stating you would kill the screws unless you got what you wanted. I do not think you made a speech in the dome, or influenced any men to fight in the stone shed on that day; that was a personal fight between two men, I am satisfied, a personal grudge. I do not believe you ordered the men from the stone shed to go in the mail bag department. There is no evidence that you were an instigator of the assembly which developed into this riot. I think this covers all the things that were worrying you, and therefore, I have been able to do what you ask me to do. Having said this, may I proceed with my formal judgment.
The evidence in this case has not changed my opinion, but rather confirmed it, as to the history of the events of the afternoon of the seventeenth of October, as expressed by me in the Kirkland trial. My opinion in this regard is, I think, well known, so I need not repeat it here. I think these things constituted a riot; more than three men were engaged in it; there was a common purpose in the minds of the men; the tranquillity of the neighbourhood was disturbed for various reasons; the assembly, although peacefully intended in its inception, soon became tumultuous; there was a promiscuous, noisy commotion which -was aggravated by some men carrying hammers, iron bars, and sticks; machines were broken, and locks were burned off doors. The warden himself was prevented from leaving, even when he desired to do so. Officers and guards were ordered to the mail bag department, and ordered to the front when shots were fired, and they felt they had to obey and did obey. Different witnesses have testified to being alarmed, to being in real fear, and these events constituted a riot.
I think I should say here, however, that the riot was not nearly so serious a matter as it was thought to have been at the time it occurred. From newspaper reports at that time, and general conversation amongst the public, it was deemed to have been an exceedingly serious matter, but I think the evidence as developed in these cases thus far has shown something different. Certainly it has convinced me that the riot was not intended to be a riot at the outset. I believe you, Buck, and the other witnesses, that the intention was a peaceful assembly, unlawful perhaps, at least breaking prison rules to do it, and the men knew they were breaking prison rules; nevertheless, I am satisfied that in the minds of the leaders anyway there was no desire that there should be a riot."
His Honour then went on to find that there was, nevertheless, a breach of the law, that Buck had participated in it, and that therefore he was guilty as charged. In dwelling with the subject of the sentence, His Honour stated as follows:
"While I do not intend to sentence you, Buck, to-day, I think at this juncture I might give some reasons which will move me in

Penitentiaries Commission Act
sentencing you when that day comes. While I am satisfied that you formed part of this riot I am also satisfied that you had an honest desire that no one should be injured and no property damaged; that is damage itself for the sake of damaging property. I am satisfied it was your desire to have the assembly of men make a demonstration merely for the purpose of emphasizing your demands for redress of grievances, and that is all to your credit. From the evidence produced in the Kirkland case I know of many of those grievances, and I know that since _ the riot they have been largely remedied, which makes your demands look reasonable; and that helps me somewhat in reaching a conclusion as to what sentence I shall impose.
While you did not personally injure any property I feel bound to hold you responsible in law, and, as I have said therefore, you are found guilty of an offence punishable with seven years, but I do not intend to give you seven years. The officer in charge of your shop says that you are the best machinist they have ever had in that shop; that your work and conduct have been commendable, and this is also very much to your credit. Then you exercised some restraint over the men, you and two or three others at certain points in this riot, and that is very much to their credit and yours."
And in another place His Honour stated:
"First, the riot itself was not of a very serious type. I would like the public to get that, because I am satisfied the public had the wrong idea of this riot at the time it occurred. The intention of the men at the outset was only to break a prison rule for the sake of assembling to make a protest, but it developed into a real riot, although not of an intensely serious nature. There have been many riots in many prisons, of a much more serious nature than this one. As riots go, I would say this was a very mild riot, but it was a riot, and I had to find you guilty of participating in it.
Then, secondly, I do not believe you instigated the riot, and that, I think, is one of the things you wanted me to find. I believe that you had an honest desire that no harm should come to either person or property. But, as I said before, being a part of the unlawful assembly which developed into a riot, you are responsible for the consequences of the riot, and I must sentence you to some term of imprisonment."
That is the judgment of Judge Deroche, delivered after a competent trial in a competent court; and in my opinion it far outweighs any evidence that may have been submitted to the superintendent by inspectors Craig and Dawson, who themselves were interested in rather minimizing or whitewashing the affair.

In a very few words I wish to emphasize again what I said yesterday in answer to the request that this matter should be postponed because the report was made at a late stage of the session, and the suggestion that it would be better that further consideration be given it by members of the house. I repeat that the bill which will be introduced merely provides for the creation of a prison board. No other change is made by the bill. This report will be considered further with the help of this prison board, when it is appointed. Any necessary changes in the law will be made then, and where such changes can be made by regulation, that will be done.
I shall go further. We, the government, on our own responsibility could propose thi3 change of policy to parliament, without the help of any report at all, even discarding this report and these recommendations. The policy is one of which we approve, and I believe that under the present circumstances, with the conditions as they exist to-day, it is very important that this prison board should be created. This is being done, and it can be done without accepting all the findings, recommendations or suggestions of the men who sat on that royal commission. We may accept all of them or any of them, but I am 
in favour of creating a prison board, without being bound to reflect against any officer or any man. It is unfortunate that the discussion on the resolution has turned to personalities instead of being directed to the necessity of a change in the system. However, as the commission itself has been assailed I may say that we are responsible for the creation and personnel of the commission. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that not one of them asked for the appointment. We tried to secure the services of the best men available, and we had difficulty in getting them- each one of them.
As the name of Mr. McRuer has been mentioned in particular, I may say that Mr. McRuer accepted, after being pressed to do so, at very considerable sacrifice to himself, as a public duty. After what has been said, I think I owe it to him to make that statement to the committee.
With regard to the report itself, I may say that all the comments of newspapers in Canada have been sent to me. There has been almost unanimity in commending the report. A few newspapers thought it was rather hard on one gentleman, but on the merits of the report itself the opinion seems to be almost unanimous. May I quote from a letter I received from the Canadian Penal Association, an organization which is doing a great service in Canada. Eminent citizens from most of the large Canadian cities serve in that association. In the brief which they have sent, in which is quoted portions of the report, they say:
In approaching you, sir, in regard to this very important document issued by what is commonly known as the Archambault (royal) commission, the officers and directors of the Canadian Penal Association wish, in the first place, to acknowledge their debt to the present government for having implemented its promises to appoint such a commission of inquiry in order to satisfy the general public on this matter of the administration of our penal system. Further, we desire to place on record our deep appreciation not only of the great and long efforts of the commission to get at the essential facts in every phase of this study, but also of the personal courtesy shown to those of us who appeared before the commission and of the sympathetic hearing given us over a year and a half ago. We are of opinion that the volume issued will be worthy of the study of every criminologist and penologist and that the general attitude on this problem enunciated by the commissioners constitutes an epoch in Canadian criminological affairs. At the same time we are quite aware that there will be strong resistance from certain quarters when it comes to legislation, but we hope the government will insist upon giving effect to the proposals made.
As I stated, all we are doing is to create a prison board. This action is not directed

Penitentiaries Commission Act
against any official. I feel inclined to answer what my right hon. friend asked about the prison superintendent. So far as I am concerned, he has certainly served faithfully during my term of office, and has been industrious. But, as has been stated, there is the difficulty of one man having in charge this huge system, one which is broadening all the time. One of the complaints made in the report was that the superintendent did not visit the penitentiary during his term of office. With the immense amount of work which is his, as head of the penitentiaries, I know he simply could not do it. This is a job for more than one man. I repeat that it is the system we are introducing to-day, and to that point I wish to limit myself. I recognize that my right hon. friend had a duty to perform, and he was loyal to a gentleman.

people of British Columbia that are affected but also the people of the prairies, because we are suffering from the same condition at the present time. It is a very undesirable condition. In every village and every polling booth in every constituency in western Canada-or at any rate in Saskatchewan and in my constituency-from four until six o'clock people flock around the radio listening to the election returns from Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. Whether the news is true or false, the returns are coming in, and people coming intending to vote are influenced. I

Elections and Franchise
do not know whether this is the best way to remedy it but this condition exists and is very undesirable, and anything that can be done to remedy it should be done.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: This matter was carefully considered in the committee, not once or twice but three times. It d'oes not appear to me that there will be suffering at either end of Canada. But it is an attempt to right a wrong which undoubtedly exists. I should very much like to see it tried. It is not such an unthinkable thing that an act should be amended when it is proved that it is not working satisfactorily. In the maritimes it does not seem to me to be an injustice that the polls should be kept open until seven o'clock. Voters do not have to wait until six-thirty to vote; they can vote when it suits them. In British Columbia, with the facilities given for voting, I cannot see that it is any deprivation of rights. This is a definite attempt to right a wrong, which has worked both ways in the past, and I think it should be tried.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
I protest against this
determination to deal with the estimated effect of advance news in the west at the expense of thousands of voters in British Columbia. I am confident that all hon. members representing constituencies on the lower mainland of British Columbia could demonstrate that it is a physical impossibility for thousands of workers there to vote before five p.m. The point has been made that modern transportation facilities enable them to travel to the polls within the space of two hours. That completely overlooks the fact that the homes of many of these workers are separated from their place of employment by Burrard inlet. It is a question not only of street car connections, but also of ferry connections. It is a question not of speed of transportation but of making definite connections at certain hours. Large communities are almost entirely populated by workers employed in Vancouver city who find it impossible to vote before six o'clock. In fact any of us who have had experience in elections on the north side of Burrard inlet know that plans have to be organized to enable the electors to reach the polls just prior to six o'clock. That is when the heaviest vote is polled. To force this clause through would definitely disfranchise whole blocks of voters in certain sections of the lower mainland of British Columbia; of that there is no doubt. Surely it is the height of folly. No one knows what the effect of advance news may be. It may be desirable to take steps
to correct that situation, but I urge the committee not to take a step which would involve the disfranchisement of thousands of voters in British Columbia.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: It is perhaps fair to explain that the special committee devoted considerable time to this question. We considered all the suggestions that were made -that of holding over the count in the maritime provinces until after the vote was polled in the west; that of changing hours; that of imposing a penalty for publishing reports. The committee concluded that whether this section as it appears in the reprinted bill goes through or not, we would at least ibe bringing to the attention of the people of Canada the need of devising some means whereby people should not be influenced by the announcement of results in some parts of Canada before the polls are closed in other parts. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for New Westminster is that we revert to the old form. While as chairman of the committee I am staying with the report of the committee and voting for the clause as it stands, I can readily understand that with opposition from both east and west the report may not be accepted.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: Replying to the statement of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), and for the information of other members of the committee, I think it only fair to point out that two hours of the day without deduction of pay are free to people employed in factories and industries to enable them to go and vote. I suggest that whether it be in Vancouver or elsewhere, with an hour available for lunch and two hours off, any voter can go to the polls and record his vote. The committee considered the possible disfranchisement of voters, and not much weight was given to that in view of the time allowed for voters to go and vote.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: Notwithstanding the two hour provision in the act I have personally known scores of voters to be disfranchised in Vancouver even at six o'clock.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
A large number of people wait until the last hour to vote. If the poll opened at seven o'clock in districts with which I am familiar, a large number would vote before eight o'clock, because they go some distance away to work and they leave about eight o'clock to be on the job at eight-thirty. Often these people do not care enough about voting to come back before six o'clock; they say: If we cannot vote before eight o'clock we are not going to vote. That happens to a large extent in British Columbia.

speechtext: As a member of the committee I was strongly opposed to the subsection and reserved my right to vote against it. I warned the other members of the committee that it would be strongly objected to by hon. members from the mari-times. As the chairman of the committee said, alternatives were considered by the committee. One I suggested myself, that the polls close at six o'clock everywhere, but that deputy returning officers in the polling divisions in the maritime provinces should not give out the results of the poll before eight o'clock. Some hon. members thought the people would be impatient to know the results, but they would get used to that. Another suggestion was to prohibit the transmission of results in the maritime provinces by radio, telegraph or telephone. Some people say there would be a leak. I think we could at any rate prevent results from being published in the newspapers. And if there should be a leak we would not be any worse off than we have been in the last fifty years. Why not try that? Why not put a provision in the act prohibiting the publication of election results in the east? If it does not work, we can come back to this synchronising of hours.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: I wish to concur in the remarks just made by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Robichaud). I cannot understand why these two alternate schemes cannot be tried. I agree with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) that it is unfair to close the polls in British Columbia as early as five o'clock, that it might disfranchise many voters; but even yet I do not understand why the results in the mari-times could not be held for two hours and why it could not be made an offence to send out news as to the results of an election until the polls have closed right across Canada. It does seem to me that would do a great deal to help the people in eastern Canada realize just how large this country is, and to remember that there is a great western part of Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext:
I come from a part of the country which is not influenced by reports either from the east or from the west, but it strikes me that if there is anything in the question now under consideration there is a difficulty either way. I quite appreciate the point made by some hon. members that by closing the polls too early you might deprive a number of working people of their opportunity to vote; but if there is anything in this contention at all it would mean that

a large number of electors wait until four o'clock to go to the polls, in order to learn what has happened at the other side of the country. There is a danger that a large number of electors may be blocked out of the polls by presenting themselves in the late hours. If that is not so, then we are not discussing anything at all, because it would only deal with a few electors who would be waiting for those results. Unless there is a large number of electors waiting for the results from the east, the question really has no practical value. So far as I am concerned I would rather favour the report of the committee closing the polls at different hours, but I would see that section 48, which requires employers to give adequate time to their employees to go and vote, was properly enforced.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: So far as the east is concerned we must take two things into consideration. The first is that in the extreme east, if we have an election in the spring or winter or fall it is practically dark at four o'clock. From four o'clock until seven o'clock it is going to be hard to keep our polls open. If a man is at a poll from eight o'clock in the morning until six o'clock at night that is long enough to ask him to stay in charge of the balloting; and in the last hour, from six to seven, there is going to be a chance for all kinds of corruption and all sorts of things to take place which may have a deleterious effect in many campaigns in that end of the country, because people are so accustomed to having the polls close at six o'clock. I am speaking from a practical point of view, and probably I am only saying what other hon. members are thinking. That is a fact. Then there is the question of expense. The candidate has to supply lunch at the noon hour, and now he will have to supply two meals.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FRANCHISE OF ELECTORS, ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS AND PRINTING AND PUBLICATION OF ELECTION DOCUMENTS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

That is all right; those are election expenses. You cannot expect a man to remain at a poll all day without something to eat, and somebody has to pay for it. I am sure the man himself is not going to do so. I am not so much concerned with that, however; I am only mentioning it as an additional cost that will have to be incurred. The geographical position is no reason why the east should be penalized and forced to hold back information which may or may not have an effect on the west or the central part of Canada. It works out the same for both parties; it does not make any difference whether it is the Libera! party, the Conservative party, the Cooperative Common-

wealth Federation or anything else. It would be an intolerable situation in eastern Canada to have the polls kept open until seven o'clock.

That was the time at which the counting and reporting was to be done. That would really mean holding the return in the polling booth, I take it. I am sorry to disagree with my hon. friend, but I do not think that is a practical means of accomplishing that end. I do not believe it is at all possible. I would not want to make any invidious comparisons between one province and another with respect to their interest in elections, but I am quite sure that in my own province, if the polls closed at six o'clock, it would be almost impossible to ask the electors, waiting outside for the results, to remain there patiently until eight o'clock, when the deputy returning officer would announce them. I fear that with
the well known public spirit of our friends from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick there would be no possibility of holding the results. Some way would be found of signalling outside. Because idle hands will find evil to do. I would be very much afraid of that. Personally, with all the desire in the world to meet the wishes of hon. members, I do not think it can be done.
The other amendment submitted to the committee is in these words:-
No person, company or corporation shall in any province before the hour of closing of the polls in such province publish the result of the polling in any electoral district in Canada, whether such publication is by radio broadcast, or by newspaper, news-sheet, poster, billboard, hand bill or in any other manner. Any person contravening the provisions of this section (and in the case of a company or corporation any person responsible for the contravention thereof) is guilty of a corrupt practice and of an offence against this act.
In the first place, the hon. member for Leeds admitted the other evening that this could be circumvented by giving the news to someone in the United States, across the river from St. Stephen, New Brunswick. Immediately it could be flashed across to the Pacific coast, and could easily be broadcast from Seattle, if anyone wished to take the trouble to get the information to British Columbia. I do not think the broadcasting of news could be prevented.
In the second place, from the point of view of public policy there would be grave objections, in that we would be seriously interfering with a free press. After all it is a serious matter, and perhaps a greater amount of abuse than that now existing would be necessary to warrant the parliament of Canada preventing newspapers from publishing accurate news. That may be allowed in some
Elections and Franchise

sections of Canada, but it should not be confirmed; nor should it be sanctioned by the parliament of Canada.

On Friday evening I did say it was possible to have a communication in the manner now outlined by the minister, and that to some extent such communication would nullify the accomplishment of the object we have in view. All I said was that we had not extraterritorial jurisdiction and could not prevent an announcement being made by radio from the city of Seattle and penetrating into British Columbia. speechtext: With the permission of the committee I would ask that section 106 be reconsidered. It deals with the question of signed pledges by candidates and prohibits a candidate from signing any sort of document that might be placed before him by the electors during an election. I think this provision goes altogether too far, because it takes away from the electors certain rights that they now possess and ought to possess. During an election a legitimate question might be asked a candidate. For instance, he might be asked whether he was in favour of railway unification, but if such a question were put to him it might involve an offence both on the part of those who put the question and on the part of the candidate himself. According to my reading of the section the electors would be prevented from asking a candidate any question along those lines. Perhaps the minister himself will admit that the section is too wide. If a request were made of a candidate for a contribution to bazaars or things of that sort, provision might very well be made against it in the statute. But when it is proposed to prevent legitimate questions being put to candidates in order to elicit an opinion on definite questions of policy, then I say it is going too far and I ask that the section be reconsidered. It should not be as drastic as it is.

This section is one which I myself suggested and therefore I am more in sympathy with it than I have been with some of the clauses for which I have been voting this afternoon. It arises out of a practice, which is too common, of certain groups, largely minorities, endeavouring to further their cause by asking candidates to sign questionnaires, pledges and so on. In my opinion that is distinctly undemocratic in that it makes of the elected member not a representative of the whole dominion but a mere delegate of a class or group or section. I may be expressing a rather old-fashioned theory of democracy, and perhaps it is; but in looking over the history of the past, from which, after all, we derive most of our institutions and some of the things that are best in life, I find that in 1774, Edmund Burke, the Irish statesman, having been confronted with a similar situation in his election in the county of Bristol, had this to say-and I think I had better quote his remarks in their entirety.
Elections and Franchise

because he states far better probably than any member of this house can the views that many of us hold. Speaking of his colleague he says:
He tells you that "the topic of instructions has occasioned much altercation and uneasiness in this city"; and he expresses himself (if I understand him rightly) in favour of the coercive authority of such instructions.
Certainly, gentlemen, it ought to be the happiness and glory of a representative to live in the strictest union, the closest correspondence, and the most unreserved communication with his constituents. Their wishes ought to have great weight with him; their opinion high respect; their business unremitted attention. It is his duty to sacrifice his repose, his pleasure, his satisfaction, to theirs; and, above all, ever, and in all cases, to prefer their interests to his own. But his unbiased opinion, his mature judgment, his enlightened conscience, he ought not to sacrifice to you, to any man, or to any set of men living. These he does not derive from your pleasure; no, nor from the law and the constitution. They are a trust from providence, for the abuse of which he is deeply answerable. Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he betrays, instead of serving, you if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
My worthy colleague says his will ought to be subservient to yours. If that be all the thing is innocent. If government were a matter of will upon any side, yours, without question, ought to be superior. But government and legislation are matters of reason and judgment, and not of inclination; and what sort of reason is that in which the determination precedes the discussion? in which one set of men deliberate and another decide? and where those who form the conclusion are perhaps three hundred miles distant from those who hear the arguments.
