speechtext:
To deliver an opinion is the right of all men; that of constituents is a weighty and respectable opinion, which a representative ought always to rejoice to hear, and which he ought always most seriously to consider. But authoritative instructions, mandates issued which the member is bound blindly and implicitly to obey, to vote and to argue for, though contrary to the clearest conviction of his judgment and conscience; these are things utterly unknown to the laws of this land, and which arise from a fundamental mistake of the whole order and tenor of our constitution.
Parliament is not a congress of ambassadors from different and hostile interests, which interests each must maintain, as an agent and advocate, against other agents and advocates; but parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation with one interest-that of the whole: where, not local purposes, not local prejudices ought to guide, but the general good, resulting from the general reason of the whole. You choose a member, indeed; but when you have chosen him, he is not a member of Bristol, but he is a member of parliament. If the local constituent should have an interest or should form a hasty opinion, evidently opposite to the real good of the rest of the community, the member for that place ought
(Mr. Power.]
to be as far, as any other, from any endeavour to give it effect. I beg pardon for saying so much on this subject. I have been unwillingly drawn into it, but I shall ever use a respectful frankness of communication with you. Your faithful friend, your devoted servant, I shall be to the end of my life; a flatterer you do not wish for.
That I think is a model of what members of parliament should write to their constituents. I read it not for the purpose of reading a lesson to hon. members, but in order to support the suggestion which I made to the committee and which is incorporated as section 106. It is based on the democratic theory and doctrine laid down by Edmund Burke, a good man in his day.

speechtext: I did not think I should have to answer Edmund Burke here this afternoon. I though the minister was a little more up to date. Edmund Burke was an illustrious statesman in his day, a hundred and fifty years ago, but conditions to-day are different. When he was seeking the favours of his constituents in Bristol the franchise was very limited. A handful of electors would elect a member of parliament. Furthermore the franchise was such that they could do almost anything they wanted in an election. In these days with adult suffrage the situation is very different. To-day everyone of the age of twenty-one and over has the right to vote, so there are more people interested in public questions than there were a hundred and fifty years ago. I am surprised that a member of the government who prides himself on his liberalism, as does the minister, should go back a hundred and fifty years for his authorities. If he desired to come a little closer home I am sure he could give a great many reasons why a clause of this kind should not be in the act, depriving the electors, as it does, of the freedom which should be theirs.	,

The only way to find out what man you want to vote for is to find out his opinions; and if some people have peculiar ideas of their own the way to find out is to ask. We can either refuse or conveniently forget or do it after the election is over, whatever is most convenient. I understand that Edmund Burke says this would lead to a man voting against his conscience. Not at all; he should not sign the paper if he is not willing to live up to it.
I would point out another matter. This is not very complimentary to our integrity. We must not sign these papers, but we can go on the hustings and promise anything, and that is all right because it is not our bond. We can make any promises, however extravagant, apparently, and get away with it; but when we are asked to put our signature to it it is all wrong, and it becomes a criminal offence. I was very much surprised when I found the clause in the bill. It is quite impracticable to force a vote on it now, because we would not get anywhere; but I should like to add my protest against this thing. I have no objection to anybody in the world coming and asking me what is my opinion, and that is really all it amounts to. But I do object to making it an offence for me to sign a paper while it is not an offence for any of these societies, some of whom I admit are cranks, to ask me to do so.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

I have to direct attention to the next item, which is statutory, covering judges' salaries and travelling allowances, amounting to S2,041,600. I want to ask a few questions. First, is there any age limit for the appointment of judges to superior courts? In my time there always was a limit, which was that the appointee should not be more than sixty years of age, the reason being that if he attained the age of seventy-five he would be entitled to superannuation, having served fifteen years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was not in the statute.

The original statute provided for fifteen years. There was no provision as to age, but in practice in the department no man over sixty was appointed to a high court position. I once urged that the most distinguished member of the bar of my own province should be appointed to the bench, but he had attained an age which the late Judge Doherty felt would mean that the established rule would be contravened, so he would not appoint him. So far as I know that rule has been honoured continuously. There have been one or two exceptions with respect to county court appointments, but not many even in that regard. To discuss the question of an appointment to the bench is sometimes regarded as something which should not take place in parliament, but I need hardly say that those who have read the life of the late Lord Darling, recently published, will quite realize that it is a proper thing to discuss. When he was appointed there was a great deal of newspaper controversy as to his fitness for the position.
Recently an appointment to the high court has been made of one well advanced towards seventy years of age, or at all events well over sixty-five, according to newspaper reports. I submit to the minister that this is not quite fair to the taxpayers of the country, having
regard to the effort that is being made to have the positions vacated by those who have attained the age of seventy-five. Obviously it means that if the position is to be vacated at seventy-five, a man appointed at the age of sixty-seven or sixty-eight years would have been only seven years on the bench. I am asking the minister whether the rule is a real one, or whether the practice has not been regarded as established sufficiently to warrant its being departed from, because I have always regarded it as a matter of very great importance? At one time the late Judge Doherty made it quite apparent that my efforts to appoint a very distinguished member of our bar must fail because the person named was sixty-five years of age at that time. Certainly that person was easily in some regards the most distinguished practitioner at our bar, and I always felt it was a very great misfortune that we were unable to appoint him, for he lived for many years after. I see the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) wonders whom I mean, and I would say that I refer to the late James Muir. The difficulty was a very real one. I should like to know what the rule, if there is any, is with respect to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There
is no fixed rule, although there has been a practice and more particularly with regard to county court judges, where the rule as to the seventy-five year age limit prevails.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It would not be in the public interest to appoint men well over sixty years who, upon reaching the age of seventy-five years, would have the right to retire on full salary, as obtains in connection with the county court judges.
A few years ago a gentleman was appointed to the bench of the county court of the county of York, I believe it was, who was well advanced in age; but in the file I found that when he was appointed the government requested that he^ sign a waiver of his right to pension. Of course friends of his have asked me not to take advantage of the wTaiver, but I have refused to intervene and he has no pension.
This year there was an appointment to the county court bench in British Columbia. Many persons were recommended, and the person I thought should receive the appointment was about sixty-five years of age. In that case, too, I declined to recommend the appointment unless the person in question signed the same sort of waiver. That was
Supply-Justice-Yukon

done. When that judge reaches the age of seventydive years he will have to retire but will not be paid a pension.
In connection with the high court there is no law compelling retirement at seventy-five years, or even making it advantageous to the incumbent to retire by drawing his full pension. The practice has always been to appoint judges not far advanced in age, or more than sixty years. I believe it would be a mistake to appoint older men not only from the point of view of the age for retirement but from the point of view of doing the work.
It is only seldom that we appoint judges over sixty years of age. There was one appointment within the last year in Ontario, and possibly that is the one my right hon. friend has in mind.
According to the press, I believe, he was sixty-seven, was he not?
He was sixty-six.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But for some years he had been engaged in quasijudicial work, and strong recommendations were made for his appointment. I knew him as a well qualified man. I may assure my right hon. friend, however, that his age was considered as an obstacle, and it was only after careful consideration that the appointment was made. The rule that barristers on their appointment to the bench should not be more than sixty years still prevails, and I shall adhere to it as far as possible.

I think no more satisfactory answer could be given than that now given by the minister. However, the appointment of a man of sixty-six years has aroused considerable discussion, especially when it was pointed out that the same gentleman was the defendant in a very difficult piece of litigation. That litigation is of so serious a character that it embarrassed his brother judges to have to deal with it.
The action was dismissed.

I know, but what has that to do with the matter? The litigation is the point I am dealing with, and the court of appeal may have to deal with it; I do not know. I think it is a bad practice to appoint to the bench one who is a party to pending litigation involving issues of grave importance.
Would the right hon. gentleman permit me to point out that the litigation was not against the particular person in question, but by virtue of his office as securities commissioner.

That is the point I make, and that is the reason why I say he should not have been appointed until the litigation was out of the way; because if the allegations contained in the statement of claim of an action of that kind were established, one would certainly hesitate to make such an appointment.
I have in mind an English case involving a judge of the court of appeal. He experienced great difficulty in that court, because the court had to decide against him in a matter of very great importance. In that instance he was not interested in the litigation when he was appointed.
I believe it is bad practice to make an appointment when litigation is pending. I have received communications of some importance with respect to the matter about which I intend to speak to the minister. It is too late to remedy the matter, so far as the appointment is concerned, but it is not too late to remedy a recurrence of a difficulty of that land. I believe the statement made by the minister is one which will be received with great satisfaction by everyone. I believe he said he will endeavour to prevent such action being taken again. I point out to him the difficulty of appointing to the bench one who is a plaintiff or defendant in litigation which will necessarily have to be considered by his brethren on the bench to which he has been appointed.
It is not always easy for a Minister of Justice to know all the facts, but I am merely directing attention to the matter so that in future he may be able to make inquiries. I believe I know how easy it is not to be fully advised of all the facts. I know of one appointment I certainly wish had not been made, and had I known certain facts which at the time I did not- know, the appointment would not have been made. The minister does the best he can, relies upon the answers he gets to the inquiries he makes, and treats them in good faith. But he is not always in a position to say, subsequently, that he has been fully advised regarding the matter, and if he has not been fully advised, a situation of great difficulty is sometimes created.
There is one other question, and it is one about which the late government experienced a good deal of difficulty. County court judges are supposed to reside, as indeed are the supreme court judges, somewhere near the point of their activities; I think it is within so many miles of a given place. The Judges Act with respect to high court judges is silent with respect to that requirement, but with respect to county court or district court judges there is such a provision, if my

Farmers' Creditors Act
memory serves me aright. A man is appointed to a position as county court judge in county X. He resides in city A. This involves the taxpayer in somewhere between $1,500 and $2,000 a year in the travelling of the judge from city A to discharge his duties in county X. Something should be done to meet such a situation.
It will be within the memory of this committee that in British Columbia an action was brought in connection with the travelling *expenses of one of the judges of the high *court, and it left an unpleasant memory. I have heard of, and in fact, I had to deal with a situation in which county court judges or district court judges made arrangements between one another so that chambers would be taken and they would thereby secure the travelling expenses incident to the discharge *of their duties outside their own jurisdiction. That is a plain and palpable disregard of the law. That, too, a minister of justice finds it difficult to know anything about unless it is brought to his attention. Circulars are sent to judges. They have been sent by [DOT]departmental officers in an endeavour to protect the exchequer, and a word of timely warning as to what the effect of this will be, and as to the power of the government to deal with it, would, I think, be desirable.
The only reason I bring these matters to the attention of the minister at this moment is that I regard them as being of great importance; because if one does a certain thing for a period, somebody else hears about it and starts in; then you have two, and then five, and then ten; ultimately you have made on the treasury a raid for which there is no *authority whatever, and this places the minister, who is entirely ignorant of the situation, in a difficult position when he has to explain, for the report of the auditor general, what authority there is for the amounts expended. Judges are in an entirely different position from others in respect to their expenses. As soon as the auditor general gets his accounts in the shape in which he requires them he pays them without question; the judge signs his little slip, puts it in the bank and gets his pay, and that is the end [DOT]of the matter. Obviously the only way a minister of justice can deal with it is by circulars and by letters addressed to the judicial bench generally, making clear what their position is under the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Travelling expenses have to be certified by the chief justice.

Oh, yes, that came about by reason of a very unfortunate case of 51952-279
which I have heard. But there is no similar provision with respect to county and district court judges, and it leaves it open to a difficulty that I shall mention privately to the minister in connection with a case where the travelling expenses of the judge had been placed at as high a figure as over 82,000 in a single year in Ontario. I was asked in a communication to bring this matter to the attention of the minister. I shall not mention any names here.

speechtext:
Is that
a case of recent occurrence?

Yes, and my attention
was directed to the page of the auditor general's report. I shall mention it privately to the minister, because I think it serves no useful purpose to mention names with respect to a matter of this sort.
There is one other matter in connection with this item that I shall perhaps be able to mention after eight o'clock.

The managers on the part of the House of Commons have the honour to report that they met in a free conference the managers on the part of the senate for the purpose of further considering Bill No. 25, intituled, "An Act to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, and the amendments thereto.

Saskatchewan and Alberta later than the thirty-first day of December, 1938: Provided that this subsection shall not apply to farmers who are soldier settlers within the meaning of the Soldier Settlement Act.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the electors of Wright county, which I have the honour to represent, I wish to congratulate and thank the government for having voted $100,000 towards expropriations and survey in view of the construction of a national boulevard in my constituency.
The construction of this boulevard has been sought for many years. I am happy to note that the government appreciates the many advantages of this important project and has seen fit to vote the money required for preliminary operations.
The proposed boulevard, which will start at the Champlain bridge on the Aylmer road, will be entirely in Quebec territory and will extend through picturesque farming country to the heights of the Gatineau mountains, the beauty and grandeur of which one can admire from these Parliament buildings by directing one's eyes beyond the Ottawa river in a north-westerly direction. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

We were discussing this

When the house rose at six o'clock I was directing attention to the next item, which is statutory, covering judges' salaries and travelling allowances, amounting to 82,041,600. I was referring to what I consider the undesirability of the appointment to the bench of an official who is the defendant in a lawsuit. He was appointed to the bench on about the thirtieth day of the trial, in the midst of his cross-examination. His appointment has certainly subjected the appointing power to a great deal of criticism. The action was brought against him alleging lack of authority in the delivery up of 275,000 shares of capital stock in one company and a larger number in another. On discovery he admitted he had no authority under the provincial statute to do this. He was a party defendant. The action was tried by, I believe, Mr. Justice McTague, and it lasted longer than any trial in the history of Ontario, so counsel for one of the parties said in a public statement. It seems to me to be rather an improper exercise of the appointing power to name a barrister who was one of the defendants in an action, under the circumstance that he was standing in the witness box in the midst of his cross-examination when the appointment was announced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not supposed to have known that.

But I am bound to say, as one of my correspondents who is uninterested says, it is pretty difficult to think it was not known at least to those from that province whose business it was to advise the minister with respect to it. He might not know it. But it does embarrass a judge in the trial of an action to have a witness in the midst of a cross-examination promoted to be his brother on the bench. It is still more embarrassing to those who have to conduct trials of actions hereafter before that very same gentleman, to find themselves in the midst of the cross-examination confronted with a new justice of the high court, he having been, when he took the witness-box, a plain member of society, known by another title, and sued in his personal capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He was defendant in his personal capacity?
Oh, yes, he was defendant in this action.
As securities commissioner.

He was sued, and it was alleged that he acted beyond his authority and was personally liable. He admitted on
discovery that he had no authority under the statute to do what he did, and in the midst of his cross-examination he suddenly became a justice of the high court. It made it very embarrassing alike for judge and counsel to face that situation.

Might I ask my right
hon. friend a question? I know he has as high regard as I have for the dignity of the judiciary of Canada, and I wondered if it would not be fair to state that it was in the official capacity in which the gentleman acted at that particular time that the question to which my right hon. friend now refers was asked.

No. My learned and
hon. friend, in a most unusual manner, has not appreciated my point.
I tried to.

It is very unusual for
him not to appreciate it. The reason is probably my lack of clarity and not his lack of understanding. What I desired to make clear was that the gentleman who was appointed to the bench was the defendant in an action, and it was alleged that he was occupying a position under a provincial statute-

May I suggest to my
right hon. friend that the fact that he was defendant in the action was possible only by reason of the official position which he occupied at that time.

If my learned and hon.
friend will possess his soul in patience, and not manifest some impatience, I shall answer him. This gentleman was a defendant, and it was alleged-properly or improperly I do not say

that he acted beyond the scope of his authority. On discovery he admitted that he had no authority to do what he did do with respect to 275,000 shares of one company and a larger number in another. The question at issue was whether or not he had made himself personally liable. In the judgment of the court different dates are given as to the duration of the trial. One of them says it lasted nine weeks; but as I understand the matter, nine weeks would include all days of the week, and the court did not sit every day of the week. The trial lasted about forty-one days, including the argument. At the end of about the thirtieth day, in the midst of his crossexamination, he suddenly became a justice of the high court, and counsel found himself

cross-examining, not a securities commissioner, but a justice of the high court, which, of course, made the situation a little difficult alike for judge and counsel.

Might I suggest to my
right hon. friend that judgment has since been given in connection with the particular action to which he refers, and that judgment is in favour of the one who was appointed.

The action was dismissed. That has nothing to do with the matter. It is as remote as the moon, and the hon. gentleman knows it, because an appeal can be taken. The difficulty is that in the midst of the cross-examination of the witness he is appointed to the bench, he himself is a party defendant, and is charged with doing something which rendered him, according to the statement of claim, personally liable. I was asked to bring this to the attention of the minister. I believe that if the Minister of Justice had known of these circumstances, he would not then have made the appointment. My long experience with him induces me to believe that he would not have made it; he would have delayed it until such time as the action was out of the road.

At this point the minister might make a short statement indicating the position of the mounted police with respect to the several provinces of Canada. It has been pointed out to me that in Nova Scotia there has been great laxity in the enforcement of the law in connection with what has always been a source of trouble, namely, smuggling. The complaint is that in that province at the present time-I daresay the minister has seen it in the press-alcohol is doctored, bottled

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
and sold as rum; that regular routes are established, and that this has been injurious to the well-being of the community at large, the practice having, moreover, become so prevalent that the present force is unable to cope with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As regards policing the provinces, we are doing only our own work in British Columbia. In Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba we are doing provincial work.
Under the agreements that have been in force for some time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. In Ontario and Quebec we have our own work under federal statutes, and under agreement we are doing work in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. I am aware of the trouble that has taken place in Nova Scotia and the complaints that have been made regarding the enforcement of statutes, especially in connection with liquor smuggling. I am advised, however, that during the last few months there have been more seizures and convictions than at any previous time, and a reorganization is being effected. I do not know whether Mr. Mead has been appointed yet, but the intention is to send him to that province. He has been doing in Montreal effective work of the kind that is necessitated in Nova Scotia. He is going there some time this summer to take charge, and it is hoped that he will do the same excellent work that he has done in Montreal.

I think that covers the question which I asked. My information is that there are fifty-two cases, of which I think I could give evidence if required, in which liquor has been landed at ports in Nova Scotia, having been really smuggled in. The minister says that he has been aware of the complaints, just as I am, and probably from the same source. For my part I should think that what he proposes to do in an endeavour to remedy the situation should be given the needed opportunity to demonstrate its usefulness, and if it is not effective, then will be the time for further criticism.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, the fact that we are sending the chief of the Montreal branch to that province is no reflection upon the officers there.
It is prima facie evidence of an intention to do the best one can.

Some time ago the minister indicated that it was the intention to investigate the complaints of espionage activities in Canada under the cloak of fascist
organization. I have seen photostat copies of letters placed in the hands of agents of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police showing that operatives are active within Canadian borders and to some extent linked up with espionage activities recently exposed in the United States. There has been considerable evidence to show that an attempt has been made to smuggle small arms into Canada, and all this has been done under the cloak of fascist organization. Can the minister make a short statement?

Before the minister
answers, I should like to say a word. A large number of documents have been sent to me, and if they are accurate they indicate clearly that there have been great activities in this dominion extending from the central provinces west. The peculiar activities touch perhaps more closely the Department of National Defence. It is not that it is regarded as likely that any effort will be made, for instance, to deal with the man power of the country, but is rather to prevent the industrial activity of the country from being made productive in munitions of war in the event of our having to produce such munitions. It is clear, for instance, that the turn of a screw might put out of commission an extremely valuable machine and render it impossible for that machine to function. The removal of a very small piece of machinery might render the whole incapable of work for a considerable time. Whether I can attach credence to these documents in their entirety I do not know, but certainly there must be considerable activity emanating from Chicago and spreading over this country dealing with conditions in Ottawa and Montreal, showing a desire to obtain information having to do with conditions in this city, with our aircraft activities, with the work that has been done in our factories. It occurs to me that we should take steps to the extent of our ability to deal with that situation. I was much impressed, when the great war came, with the fact that we laughed at the idea of any such thing as espionage in this country, and we did not take it seriously. Yet within a short time a bridge was destroyed. We were able to trace the matter and ultimately take proceedings in connection with it. The destruction of that bridge indicated a close and accurate knowledge of general conditions in this country. The placing of an explosive at a particular point wrecked the bridge. My information is that a great deal of activity is being carried on; that cameras are very much in use.
In the case I mentioned the other evening respecting a particular individual, I gave such

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
information as I had to one department which was looking into the matter for another purpose. It is clear that the gentleman had a map case, a camera and binoculars, which largely constituted his stock in trade. He worked on a farm in Ontario, and the farmer with whom he worked wrote to me. He then transferred his activities to Montreal. It is not necessary or desirable that I should at this time enter into a discussion of what he did there; that had to do with another branch of the activities of our friends.
If the evidence is to be relied on-I do not wish to say it is wholly reliable-certainly photostat copies of documents which came to me clearly indicate that we have in our midst in this country a condition which we should not tolerate. I trust the minister will see that the police take every step in their power to prevent this from continuing. We should cooperate as far as possible with the United States, because it is reasonably clear that the master minds that control activities there are also controlling them here. The communications to which I refer were directed to Chicago, and the difficulties that had to 'be overcome to obtain the information were great. It is desirable that we should not have any condition prevailing which would render ineffective any measures we might desire to take, or which would cripple our hands if we desired to use our army or air force for our own defence in time of peril. I was struck by reports as to what had been done in some of the great industrial organizations. No one thinks for a moment that there is an effort to cripple our man power in the large sense, but there appears to be an effort to cripple those productive machines on which in mechanized war the people must rely for their defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In answer, first to the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), I may say the communications he has received have also been received by me and by the department, and inquiries have been made. This allegation that people in Montreal who call themselves fascists were drilling and having arms arose, first, through statements in the press from boastings on the part of the so-called leaders, seekers after publicity more than anything else, that they had 25,000, 30,000 and, some were cheerful enough to say, 75,000 adherents. The number is much less than that. Well-intentioned people, even eminent gentlemen, by believing that sort of thing and giving expression to fear about it, are rather playing into the hands of those so-called fascist leaders who seek publicity. It is the same 
with the communists; they want publicity; if they do not get it they disappear. They live on it. We found that there was nothing as far as those allegations as to arms are concerned. Some of these people congregate in large numbers with all the paraphernalia, shirts-I do not know whether black or brown; it is foolish anyway-and make gestures and that sort of thing. They do, fifteen or twenty or twenty-five of them, what they call military exercises, just stand at attention and walk. There is nothing very dangerous about it, except that they make inflammatory speeches, denouncing many public men, particularly your humble servant. One of them said at a meeting that when they take office the first Jew that will be expelled from Canada will be Ernest Lapointe. But this does not prevent me from sleeping at night.
As far as reports that they were importing arms are concerned, these were sent to us by certain gentlemen, who were found by the agents of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to be members of the communist party. We followed the hints and suggestions that were given to us from those men, but at the last moment the people were always disappearing, and the police officers who went to the places indicated discovered that there was nothing there. So the denunciations of those gentlemen will not be taken very seriously in the future unless they are supported by something more definite.
My remarks in that regard apply both to communists and fascists. They live on publicity, notoriety; they like it to be said that there are 50,000, 100,000 of them; that they are going to have candidates everywhere at the next general election-
That may account for the Kingston riots.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It may. But I implore my fellow citizens not to be alarmed by these reports which are given to the press and at meetings by people who want to be considered big men and important factors in the national life. If we judged by press reports, Montreal is a place where we are in serious danger from both sides, fascists and communists. Let me tell hon. members that we are not afraid of them there. The population is too sane to be carried away by those crazy appeals. On the other hand I may assure the committee that the police and the secret service of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have the situation well in hand. If anything of a serious nature, or suggesting any danger, should happen, these people will find that Canada is not a place where such things can be carried on without interference by the police.

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
That does not touch my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In reference to the subject matter of the remarks of my right hon. friend, while it would not be in the public interest to divulge what steps are being taken, or by which department, there again I can assure him that the situation is being looked after and is well in hand.
I do not and we do not minimize the possible danger of the situation which my right hon. friend has depicted; we will collaborate and are collaborating not only with the United States but also with the British authorities in that respect.

I am not attempting to exaggerate the importance of the fascist organization; but the situation took a different turn when a number of individuals were indicted during the grand jury sessions in the United States recently where, as I am informed, it was definitely shown that there was a relationship between those activities in the United States and similar activities in and around our important airports in Canada. I am asking the minister to exercise some restraint on organizations professing fascism, but which actually are commonly used as a cloak for espionage activities on the part of agents of foreign governments. May I ask if there has been some cooperation between the departments of Canada and the United States in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
So that these individuals may not cross the border and embarrass us with their activities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I quite understand what my hon. friend has in view. For a time this session I considered the introduction of legislation similar to that enacted in Great Britain a couple of years ago, prohibiting parading in uniform for political purposes. I did not recommend it to the government, however, because I thought really it was giving too much importance to these people. There is some danger of doing that, and it is just what they want. If necessary, however, I shall be pleased to submit legislation of that kind to parliament if this movement increases; but in spite of the boasts appearing in their own little newspapers, my information, based upon facts ascertained by our agents, is that, instead of the movement spreading, the leaders find it difficult to gather at their meetings the same number of people who were attracted there by curiosity at first. However, we are looking after the matter.

If it were not for the fact that I think every member of the committee should have a clear appreciation of the possible seriousness of the matter to which the hon. member for Vancouver North has referred, as well as the statement I have made,
I should have been content merely to leave it to a private conversation with the minister. But I think every member of the committee should have some conception of what I regard as the seriousness of the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The subject matter of the remarks of my right hon. friend is much more important.

I must say that in the main I do not disagree with the minister in the other matters to which he has referred; but with respect to the question of espionage and spies, in the Niagara area, shall I say, the evidence submitted to me indicated that an effort was being made to bring over three hundred revolvers, and the person named upon whom they were to rely to effect the transfer across the border enjoyed the reputation of a well known bootlegger and smuggler, whatever that may mean.
I mention that now in this committee not because I do not think the minister is seized with the seriousness of it, or because I do not know that at least one other department, if not more, is concerned about it, but because I think it desirable that every member of the committee should hear the statement the minister has made, and that the members of the committee, when they leave here, should have a clear appreciation of just what may be involved. I think the statement of the minister will do much to help all of us realize, as we in this country should realize, that there is a possibility of this becoming a serious matter, though in the main we have always treated these questions as being unworthy of very serious attention. From what has taken place in the United States it now appears that something of the same sort is going on in at least some parts of this country, and if once we make it known in this public way that this is not to be permitted to continue with impunity, I think that in itself will have a very salutary effect; for I am satisfied that if the police and other branches of government departments take the matter in hand, we can adequately deal with it.

I want to assure the hon.
member for Vancouver North that what the Minister of Justice has said in connection with the fascist movement in the district of Montreal and the province of Quebec is quite correct. The so-called leaders of that

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
movement, particularly in the district of Montreal, are in no way leaders in the real sense of that term. They are men of very ordinary talent who love to wear a uniform of some distinctive character; and finding no other possible way of wearing such a uniform except through the medium of a movement such as this fascist movement, they don that uinform and pretend to be leaders. Now they are even quarrelling among themselves as to which is the actual leader and which the captain of this so-called movement, which has very little significance in the province of Quebec. It has been given wide publicity outside that province, much to the detriment of Quebec, but conditions have been very much exaggerated even in comparison with what they were at the maximum of their intensity.
A year or two ago I think we instituted something in the way of a cadet scheme or a training system for prospective members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I know there is a training school at Regina; but this system was introduced in order to train young men as prospective members of the police, or at least to give them the training which would be necessary to permit them to become established in that force. I was wondering if that effort had been pursued to any great extent. I think it was an excellent move. Even if it is not possible to absorb these young men into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, they have been excellently trained for other purposes, and may be trained to such an extent that they could find places in the service of a provincial or municipal government, or even with industrial plants. The training they would receive under a cadet system or the training system of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would not only fit them for that force, but fit them admirably for a position elsewhere in life. I was wondering if that system, instituted at one time, was meeting with any favourable progress, or whether it had been discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I agree
with what the hon. member has stated with regard to the excellence of the initiative taken to train some young men as prospective members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Last year at a certain time there were 300, and I believe the average was about 175 or 180. I am not sure that this will be done this year, as the money at our disposal is being used for additional reinforcements in some parts of the country. I have a question to ask the minister and a bit of advice to offer him, if he will kindly listen to me. The Public Archives Department publishes each year a most interesting report, but in addition it publishes from time to time special reports which should be better known to the public. I refer particularly to the work entitled Constitutional Documents whose authors are Messrs. Short and Doughty. These volumes have been published three times. The first English edition was brought out in 1907, with a French translation in 1911; the second English edition was published in 1914, with a French translation in 1915, and the third1 and last edition was printed in English in 1918 and in French in 1921. I have tried to obtain copies for every school in my constituency, but I was told that the quantity available did not permit of a public distribution. I managed, however, to get three copies of the series-one English and two French. I placed them in three of the principal schools of my constituency.
It is my opinion that this work should be reprinted with a view to being placed in the hands of all educators and of all citizens who take an interest in Canadian history. I do not expect the minister to promise this very evening to have these volumes reprinted immediately, but I ask him to give favourable consideration to my request in order that, copies may be obtained next year.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:

vote for increased facilities at the hospital mentioned by the hon. member. I am glad to see the
increase for this purpose, but could the minister tell us briefly the nature of the increased services to the Indians for the eradication of tuberculosis?

That is done in cooperation with the provincial departments of health, and consists mainly of surveys in Indian schools, particularly in the older settled communities. Is it under this vote that,
buildings are erected or provision made at the different schools to take care of cases which are under suspicion?

The vote covers Indian
hospitals.

The minister told us that
this had to do with inspection of schools; that the provincial authorities send out their medical men and carry on these clinics at the Indian schools and settlements. Is provision made at each of these schools to take care of suspects?

I did not get the import
of my hon. friend's question before. The matter presents some difficulty. An effort is being made where possible to segregate Indian children who are active tubercular cases where they can receive treatment and possibly some instruction at the same time. We hope to make some progress this year, perhaps by taking one school and centring the active tubercular cases in it for treatment. But it is not intended under this vote to build institutions for the care of tubercular cases.
Is it not being done at the present time and for the past two years at Coqualeetza school at Sardis, and St. Mary's school at Mission City?

There are a few cases
where preventoria have been built. These are for cases that may be potential spreaders of the disease among other children. These cases are isolated in the preventoria. That may be extended in a few instances this year.

I understand that has been very successful at these points. As soon as a child in the school is under suspicion, it is removed to the preventorium, and in discussion with the medical men they speak very highly of the policy and recommend that it should be continued and extended.

There will be a few of
those preventoria opened again this year for that purpose. I think there is one at Alert Bay, British Columbia, and one at Fort Alexander in Manitoba.

The problem of tuberculosis among the Indians is one which, I am sure, is engaging the attention of the department. It has for a long time engaged the attention of the Canadian Tuberculosis Association and of organized medicine. I should like to place before the committee a memorandum setting out the viewpoint of organized medicine with reference to the problem of tuberculosis particularly among the Indians.
Last year in Canada there were 6,763 deaths from tuberculosis. Of that number 748 were among the Indian population. That is, 11 per cent of the deaths in this country
Si ipp ly-In dian Affairs

from tuberculosis occurred among the Indian population. That figures out at twelve times as many per 100,000 of population among the Indians as among the white people. That means that the Indian death rate, which was ten times as many in 1936, has now risen to twelve times as many per 100.000 as among the white population. This is the memorandum :
The medical services of the Indian Affairs branch, however complete they may be and deserving of commendation in other ways are singularly lacking and inadequate in the matter of control of tuberculosis. A more aggressive policy is absolutely necessary to solve this problem. A comprehensive and progressive program is long overdue. These observations are based upon the following facts:
1.	The Canadian people have failed in their duty to 112,000 Indians as long as they are denied facilities for the diagnosis and treatment of tuberculosis to the same degree as they are available for the white population.
2.	The failure to control tuberculosis in the Indian population is hampering the program among the white population. Canadian provinces have assumed responsibility for tuberculosis control in their white population and they are complaining of the handicap due to the lack of an aggressive policy on the part of the dominion government for the Indian.
3.	The provincial health departments feel that it is unfair and inexcusable that a menace is allowed to exist in a section of the population within their boundaries which is not subject to the same measures of control that the provinces have found necessary to establish for the remainder of their people.
4.	Considerable sums of money are spent every year on education, relief and general medical services for Indians, but little is spent on tuberculosis, the Indians' chief cause of death, and by far the greatest cause of illness in the Indian population.
There are two reasons why a policy of tuberculosis control has not been initiated. We propose to discuss these and to suggest in a general way their remedies.
1.	Sufficient money has never been voted by parliament to make a worth while program possible. It is urged that the usual appropriation be supplemented by a sum of $300,000, the minimum required for a general tuberculosis program, and that in addition $200,000 be voted for a two year construction program to provide accommodation in areas where no facilities are available.
2.	Those under whose jurisdiction the Indians fall have told us that a reasonable long term policy with respect to Indian tuberculosis has not yet been enunciated. We would like to state that methods of control of tuberculosis in the white population are now clearly outlined and accepted and are being followed with outstanding success. The methods that should be followed in the Indian population can be no less clearly outlined. Their application may require some adaptation to Indian conditions, but the fundamental principles are the same.
In the campaign against tuberculosis in the white population it has become necessary to

define clearly the relative importance of predisposing and exciting causes of tuberculosis. It is our belief, that in the past, undue importance has been attributed to racial susceptibility, climate, diet and other environmental factors. This has served to becloud the real issue, namely that tuberculosis is a communicable disease, in the same way that leprosy, typhoid fever or smallpox are communicable diseases.
Measures to improve the housing, diet and other environmental status of the Indian are worthy of commendation but these measures will fail unless the communicable nature of the disease is recognized, and measures taken to control the spread of infection. The tubercle bacillus, always was, is and always will be the cause of tuberculosis, and hence direct measures are necessary to localize or segregate the germ. These measures will have far more value than indirect methods which are unavailing in the presence of massive infection by tubercle bacilli. Tuberculosis comes from tuberculosis.
We believe that the main reason why the Indian is polluted with tuberculosis is because he is conceived, born, educated, lives and dies in an atmosphere of tuberculosis. This atmosphere of tuberculosis infection wras grafted upon the Indian by his first contact with white settlers and has continued ever since.
When one realizes that the white population of this country has been the source of tuberculosis among the Indian population, it becomes clear and definite that the obligation is upon the government of this country to see to it that the Indians, who are their wards and for whom we have a contractual and moral obligation, are given the attention which they deserve for this disease in particular.
Whatever possibilities of escaping from this menace were possible when the Indian lived an open, nomadic life, were removed when he became firmly established on reserves. The faults of environment which have developed may have served to aggravate but are not the real cause of tuberculosis.
It is common knowledge that the Indian has never been given the means to protect himself from this menace in the same manner that has been afforded the more fortunate white population. A policy of tuberculosis control should recognize these facts as fundamental and the lines to be followed based on the most practicable and reasonable manner in which this lack can be overcome.
The policy of control should proceed from two premises:
1.	That the recognition or diagnosis of the disease is necessary wherever it exists in the Indian population. It was imperative that these diagnostic facilities be developed for the white population. This service should be made available for the Indian population also. Provincial clinics are even now available and are being utilized in a limited way but could be made more useful by proper organization. This requires the addition of trained personnel on the staff of the Indian affairs branch to coordinate and organize these diagnostic facilities.

Supply-Indian Affairs
I just wonder if any progress has been made during the last year towards the setting up of any such branch in the department.
It requires the addition of one or more physicians trained in tuberculosis to organize this work among the Indians in Canada. It is suggested that it requires one for the east and one for the west.
Such a system would lead to the proper notification and recording of tuberculosis on the Indian reserves. This is the foundation for a tuberculosis control program for any community or group of people.
2.	The next is that some action be taken in regard to cases of tuberculosis that are found to exist. This should be done by training. supervision, treatment or segregation.
We believe that in by far the greater number of recognized cases, some action could be taken that would gradually lessen the incidence of infection. This might be brought about in several ways and we offer the following suggestions that could be followed depending on the type of case that is found to exist:
1.	In the school. The age of greatest incidence of tuberculosis in the Indian is in the 'teen age group in contrast to the white where it is greatest in the 20-30 group.
I would direct that particularly to the attention of the minister, that the greatest incidence of tuberculosis in Indians is in the school age group, whereas the greatest incidence in the population other than Indian is between the ages of twenty to thirty. That elearty brings to mind the necessity of tackling this problem in the schools.
For this reason coordinated diagnostic services of the provincial tuberculosis clinics and the trained diagnostic staff of the Indian affairs branch should regularly examine the school children at yearly intervals. Cases of tuberculosis would thus be recognized and dealt with in two ways:
(a)	By removing open spreaders to a sanatorium or hospital.
(b)	Minimal early cases who are potential spreader's could be economically cared for in separate schools or divisions of existing schools where their education could be continued. They do not require expensive care.
In this connection this policy is already in operation by the Indian affairs branch in a limited way. It is found to be feasible, and has already shown evidence of controlling and reducing tuberculosis in the school population. It is the one bright spot in an otherwise dark picture. But it cannot be successful without further measures to control infection on the reserves. In the past some of these children have been sent back to the reserves to receive further infection and in turn to infect the pre-school population.
2.	On the reserves. Extension of the diagnostic services will bring to light the extent of the problem in the general reserve population. Cases that are so discovered should then be dealt with. Surveys are useless unless followed up. It seems reasonable that these will fall into several groups:
(a) Those that cannot be dealt with in any way but on the reserves. These will be the
older members of the band in whom old customs and traditions are so strongly ingrained that they either cannot be persuaded or that it would be inhumane to suggest that they be removed from the reserve. Some determined effort must be made on the reserve by Indian agents, medical officers, or health nurses, to provide as much segregation as possible. We recognize the old objections that will be raised that it is impossible but it can and must be done as it has been done even in slum areas in the white population. This requires a particular type of nurse with aptitude and training. In this connection, public health officials and tuberculosis officers maintain that there is a field for public health nurses and that they can make a contribution to this problem at a relatively small cost. They maintain that the limited staff of nurses employed by the Indian affairs branch prior to 1932 were doing creditable and worthwhile work. It is our belief that this avenue of attack should be further explored.
(b) The actual segregation of those in which this line should be followed. The segregation of tuberculous patients is a weapon believed to be most powerful in controlling tuberculosis in any community be it white, black or Indian. It is our considered opinion that the Indian affairs branch should treat and maintain in tuberculosis institutions that have been established, or that are feasible to establish, a reasonable number of tuberculous Indians for the protection of the whole Indian population. Experience will determine the number that should be so treated, but for the present a minimum of two hundred should be segregated. This will first include cases from those parts of Canada where the Indian population is in close contact with white people, and hence will contribute to the solution of the problem in both the white and Indian communities.
This group will include young Indians who are at present health minded and are asking for such treatment, cases from large families where there are numbers of contacts, hopeful eases that can be cured, intelligent Indians whose education and sanitary habits will have some effect in raising the .standards of the Indian generally. To deny that this is possible is a negation of the assumption that there is any use whatever in the policy of the Indian affairs branch of education of the Indian in any capacity.
The question of where this segregation should be given is an important one. It is natural and logical, just as it is in the white population, that this treatment and segregation be carried out as near as possible to the population it serves. This leads us to the question of reserve hospitals, or small so-called cottage sanitoria. If the Indians were in sufficiently large groups that these institutions might be practicable or economically possible this would undoubtedly be advisable. Its value has already been demonstrated by the Indian hospital at Fort Qu'Appelle, and other Indian hospitals easily accessible to reserves where already a certain number of tuberculous patients have been successfully segregated, and have been persuaded to remain for treatment with a minimum of difficulty. A satisfactory number of these cases have made a successful recovery. It is possible that in some instances this could
Supply-Indian Affairs

be adopted where there are large aggregations of Indians, but it is also true that where there are large aggregations of Indians beds are available in provincial sanitoria, such as Ontario and Saskatchewan, and a policy of duplicating these beds might receive serious objection as to the advisability of spending public funds in their construction. For the many scattered small Indian reserves local cottage sanitoria would seem to be out of the question.
Some general observations which would appear to influence to some extent the policy of treatment and segregation might be made. One is that considerable differences exist between the Indians east of the great lakes and those to the west of the great lakes. Those east of the great lakes have been longer in contact with the white population, there is a greater admixture of white blood, they approach more nearly to the standards of white man, and what is more important their tuberculosis death rate is less than half of that which obtains in the western provinces.
Nothing could more clearly demonstrate the usefulness of the program which has been carried on east of the great lakes and the lack of program which has not been carried on west of the great lakes.
Carried.

There is plenty of time. This is a very important subject, and if this country is going to perform a moral and contractual obligation to the 112,000 Indians in the country, then it is well worth giving some time to the consideration of their health.
For them, segregation and treatment in the white men's sanatoria would seem to be preferable where this can be obtained. There is .also the general observation that control policies will be more difficult to apply to the northern Indians, as they are so much in contact with the white people. For this reason, policies *of control should be instituted first in those parts oif the country where the Indian is in contact with others.
It is our firm conviction after years of thought and discussion that such a policy _ as we have outlined, if pursued over a period of years, would substantially reduce tuberculosis among the Indians. It would remove the growing criticism of the Indian affairs branch and of the Canadian government for what is generally considered a breach of trust in our obligation to a submerged and conquered race.
I should like briefly to summarize the financial requirements for such a program. The figures can be summarized under the following headings: Additional medical personnel, $15,000; extension of nursing service, $20,000; cost of continuation and expansion of school surveys and general diagnostic work, $75,000, and treatment of tuberculous Indians in sanatoria or hospitals, $190,000, making a total cost of $300,000.
These figures have been detailed with respect to the various provinces.

I wish to emphasize the importance of this particular problem. If one wished to take a selfish view it would be this, that the white population is being continually re-infected from the Indian population, where they are in close contact with one another. The death rate among the Indians is twelve times as great as among the white population. Statistics for last year show that the number of deaths in Canada was 6,763, whereas among the Indians it was 748. In other words, approximately twelve times as many Indians per 100,000 of population died of tuberculosis as died among the whites. Two years ago there were only ten times as many, so that, instead of lessening, the problem is gaining headway.
The Canadian Tuberculosis Association and organized medicine from one end of the country to the other feel, as I said a year ago, that the splendid work which has been done through the years by the organization is being nullified through lack of work on the part of the Indian Affairs branch. I am not criticizing the minister or his officials particularly. I know they find it difficult to persuade the Minister of Finance and other members of the government as to the importance of the problem, and find further difficulty each year in obtaining an appropriation sufficient to combat the disease.
AH I do at this time is to lend a word of [DOT]encouragement to the government, and to express appreciation of the work which has already been inaugurated in the Indian Affairs branch in connection with this phase of the matter. I would wish the minister continued success, and would hope that from year to year he might attack the problem more vigorously and might be successful in obtaining a greater appropriation to carry on the work. I would hope that he might extend the personnel of his department to include trained and efficient experts in tuberculosis, so that he might render a first-class service to those under his care, and so that he might give that measure of protection to the white population living adjacent to the Indian reserves to which they are entitled and of which they are deserving.

As the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) has said, the problem is an extremely important one, and I am grateful to him for the statement he has just made. In view of his experience I am sure any observations from him will be found useful in the department.
When I succeeded in inducing my colleagues to increase the medical vote for the Indians, I did so for the purpose of making an attack on tuberculosis among the Indians. The importance of the problem has not been over-

emphasized by the hon. member. As the committee will recall, a year ago there was a small appropriation for a preliminary survey in some of the Indian schools. That survey revealed an appalling state of affairs in many of the schools.
The vote this year is approximately $300,-
000.	When we gave consideration to the question of how it could be most effectively spent, the department called into consultation the best tuberculosis authorities that we had in each of the provinces, and I wish to state publicly my appreciation of the services that they rendered. The line of attack which the department is now following carries with it the endorsation of these medical authorities who have had to do mainly with tuberculosis problems among the whites in each of the provinces. That program is directed, first, towards the schools where surveys are made, and active cases of tuberculosis, as well as potential spreaders, removed to sanatoria that may be adjacent to the schools. Every effort is made to segregate those who may be a source of infection. The program extends also to treatment in sanatoria of the more active cases from the reserves.
The allocation of the expenditure for this year falls roughly under three or four heads which pretty well coincide with the suggestions made by the hon. member for Renfrew South. It is proposed to add a tuberculosis trained man to the medical staff in the head office administration at Ottawa. The expenditure for medical men and public health nurses associated with the control of tuberculosis amounts to over $14,000; travelling expenses amount to between $10,000 and $11,000. Fees for diagnostic specialists and clinics employed in tuberculosis surveys, on the basis of ten thousand Indians to be examined, account for $30,000. There is a further provision for the examination of pupils who are found to have minimal tuberculosis in the Indian schools, a small allowance, amounting to $45,000 is made for their extra care and for food, over and above the tuition fees. For the maintenance of existing sanatoria and hospitals for Indians suffering from active tuberculosis there is the sum of approximately $190,000. I think it may be said that this is the first definite attack which has been made upon the problem among the Indian population.
As I said a moment ago, we have had the fullest cooperation from the provincial authorities, and certainly my conception of the method to be followed is to work in the closest cooperation possible with the health authorities in all the provinces who have more immediately under their charge the treatment of tuberculosis among the white population. I
think we have made a fair start. It is quite true that more funds could be used if they were available, and it may be found possible to increase the vote next year based on the information we gather in regard to this problem during the present year. I would hope so, because there is no doubt that tuberculosis among the Indians has a definite relationship to the health of the white population. I hope, indeed I am sure, that we shall get satisfactory results from the expenditure we are making this year.
